Major Bank Outages Across The US

First Microsoft, then the airlines, and now some of America's biggest banks.

Reports are coming in today of widespread service disruptions across JPMorganChase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, U.S. Bank, and Capital One, with thousands of customers struggling to access their accounts. Payment platform Zelle® is also reportedly experiencing issues.

This comes just days after Microsoft's outage last week and a weekend of major disruption across U.S. airlines.

There is no confirmed connection between these incidents, but the timing certainly raises some questions.

We have become incredibly dependent on digital infrastructure, and when something goes wrong, the disruption can spread quickly. Whether it's banking, travel, healthcare, or everyday business operations, the consequences are becoming harder to ignore.

I've spoken before about cybersecurity being one of my biggest investment themes heading into 2027, and events like these only reinforce that view.

It's not just about protecting against cyberattacks anymore. It's about resilience, infrastructure security, and ensuring that critical systems can continue operating when things go wrong.

As businesses continue to move more of their operations into the cloud and AI becomes increasingly embedded in everything we do, the importance of securing that infrastructure is only going to grow.

I think cybersecurity will remain one of the most prominent investment themes throughout 2027, and potentially well beyond.

The more connected the world becomes, the more valuable it is to keep those connections secure and operational.

I’ve turned my AML case study series into a newsletter: Beyond the Checklist.
It starts from one question: what separates a compliance programme that exists on paper from one that works? The first three parts cover Bank of America, Rabobank, and how you prove a control works. Next come how AML works day to day, how it applies in India, and the technology behind it.
I’m early in this field, so corrections and perspectives from practitioners are very welcome.

⚠️ If an AI agent gets compromised while interacting with your web app, who holds the bag? According to major US banks this week—the user does.

Over the last 24 hours, Citi, PNC, and Citizens updated their customer terms—following JPMorgan and Bank of America—to shift financial liability for third-party AI agent hacks directly onto account holders. At the same time, Anthropic just closed its historic Nasdaq debut at a $1.3T+ valuation, proving autonomous AI workflows are rapidly becoming standard infrastructure.

When financial liability shifts to the end user, **Frontend UX & Confirmation Design** stops being just "nice to have" and becomes the primary line of consumer protection.
Here is how modern frontend engineering needs to design for high-stakes human oversight:

* 🛑 **Intentional Friction for Destructive or Financial Actions:** We spent a decade optimizing for "1-click" everything. When an AI agent or automated workflow triggers a transfer, permission change, or checkout, UI patterns need deliberate confirmation checkpoints—clear visual diffs showing *what* is changing, *who* initiated it, and *how* to undo it before commitment.

* 🔑 **Passkeys & WebAuthn Over Session Tokens Alone:** When third-party agents act on a user's behalf via delegated sessions, hardware-backed step-up authentication (WebAuthn / Passkeys) inside the browser ensures critical mutations still require cryptographic human presence.

* 🪟 **Transparent Audit Trails in the UI:** Users shouldn't have to dig through raw logs to see what an integrated assistant or extension just did in their session. Surfacing real-time, human-readable activity feeds with TypeScript-enforced action schemas builds trust and catches anomalies before damage spreads.

💡 **Actionable Takeaway:**
Frictionless UX is great for browsing, but **verifiable UX** is essential for transactions. As AI agents take on more user agency, frontend developers are the architects of the final human checkpoint.

Where do you draw the line between seamless automation and intentional UI friction in your apps? Let’s discuss in the comments! 👇

#WebDevelopment #Frontend #UXDesign #ReactJS #NextJS #TypeScript #AIEngineering #WebAuthn #TechNews2026

Three major US banks just changed their terms: if an AI agent gets hacked, the loss is yours.

Citi, PNC and Citizens updated their terms this week. Customers are now responsible for anything a third-party AI agent does in their accounts, even after leaked credentials or a hacked agent. JPMorgan and Bank of America reportedly went first.

Read that again as a developer.

Agents are getting real access to money, data and infrastructure. Nobody has agreed yet on who's liable when one goes wrong.

What I'd build into any agent feature today:

• Least-privilege access, read-only by default
• Hard limits on spending and actions
• Human approval for anything irreversible
• A full audit log of every action
• Short-lived tokens, never long-lived passwords

The next big skill isn't building agents that can do more. It's building agents that can safely do less.

When an AI agent makes a costly mistake, who should pay: the user, the company, or the developer who built it? 👇

#AIAgents #AISecurity #SoftwareEngineering #Cybersecurity #ArtificialIntelligence

👀 Zelle® just sent $1.25M in its first confidential stablecoin transfer on Solana.

And this one matters for banks.

The bank-owned payments network demonstrated a $1.25M transfer using its new stablecoin, ZelleUSD (ZLUSD), live on stage at Solana Breakpoint: https://lnkd.in/dgenjXnv

Here’s what happened:

→ ZelleUSD was issued to a bank by Anchorage Digital
→ The balance was switched to confidential
→ $1.25M was transferred to another bank
→ The receiving bank decrypted the transaction
→ The amount remained hidden on-chain while the transfer itself stayed verifiable

Important caveat: this happened on Solana devnet, so this was a technology demonstration rather than a live production payment.

But look at who is behind Zelle:

Bank of America.
Capital One.
JPMorgan Chase.
PNC.
Truist.
U.S. Bank.
Wells Fargo.

ZelleUSD is issued by Anchorage Digital Bank and runs on Solana. 

And privacy could be a BIG part of the story here.

One of the biggest objections banks have had to public blockchains is obvious: they don’t want balances and transaction amounts visible to everyone.

Confidential transfers potentially change that equation.

As Zelle’s Alexandra Lang put it:

“We're here to deliver payments at scale, and Solana presents the features and the growing stablecoin ecosystem that gives us a great place to build.”

ZelleUSD isn’t live for consumers yet.

But one of America’s biggest bank-owned payment networks is now publicly demonstrating how its own digital dollar could move between banks on a public blockchain.

Stablecoins are getting very, very close to the heart of traditional banking. 👀

🎬 How can HR prepare for jobs that don't yet exist?

That question sits at the heart of Series 58 of the Digital HR Leaders podcast. Across five conversations, we explored why preparing for an uncertain future requires more than predicting tomorrow's jobs and skills.

As AI reshapes work, HR needs to build organisations where people can learn, adapt, develop relationships and move into opportunities we cannot yet fully describe.

A few insights that stood out:
1️⃣ Jack Buckley on how Roblox assesses future talent
🎙️ “We are trying to move away from traditional coding tests to a way to measure computational thinking.”

2️⃣ Michael Arena and Greg Pryor share insights from The New Social Code on relationships
🎙️ “Don't design your connections and your network for what you're doing today, design it for what you want to do tomorrow.”

3️⃣ Loïc Michel 💎 on skills intelligence
🎙️ "Better visibility of internal skills helped SNCF reduce annual subcontractor spending by €100 million."

4️⃣ Dr. Sebastian Wernicke on better decisions
🎙️ “The purpose of data is to act differently and to decide differently.”

5️⃣ Sonia FOSSE on workforce agility
🎙️ “Knowing the skills of our people brings a lot more value to everybody, to them, to our company, to our customers.”

Also included is a bonus episode with Michael Wynn and Himanshu Palsule on building an AI-ready workforce at Bank of America.

🙏 Thank you to our guests, and to 365Talents, a Docebo company, for sponsoring the series.

Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo and U.S. Bank customers spent Monday locked out of their accounts. By early afternoon, Downdetector showed more than 4,300 reports for Chase alone, and none of the banks had said what went wrong.
 
This is the third major outage in four days. Microsoft went down last week, and on Friday the FAA grounded every flight in the country. We leaned toward an AI explanation on Friday because the FAA had just rolled out a new AI traffic tool. The cause turned out to be a contractor replacing a router at a remote site.
 
So we’re not guessing about the banks. When several banks fail at once, a shared vendor is usually one of the first suspects, but nothing has been confirmed yet.
 
The outages we can explain so far came from routine changes to complicated systems. Banks are now adding AI to those same systems, which makes it harder to tell what broke. On the day something goes down, leaders should be able to say what changed in the last 24 hours and which vendors sit in the path of their core services. If that takes a day to figure out, speculation fills the gap.

October's regulatory actions send a clear message: The question is no longer whether you have controls, but whether they work.

Looking across October's developments in sanctions and AML, one theme stands out.

Regulatory expectations are shifting from the existence of policies, procedures and controls to their actual effectiveness.

A few developments worth noting:

- Sanctions: The EU expanded its listings and targeted sanctions circumvention networks. OFAC continued its focus on sanctions evasion, while the UK introduced new designations and human rights sanctions measures.
- AML: FATF's plenary outcomes, AMLA's work on regulatory technical standards, and developments around MiCA highlight the growing focus on consistent, risk-based financial crime controls.
- Enforcement: The Bank of America BSA/AML findings, FCA action against firms with AML control deficiencies, and enforcement actions involving transaction monitoring and suspicious activity reporting reinforce the same message.
- Crypto: The record-breaking Binance-related hack and continued regulatory scrutiny of virtual assets bring sanctions evasion, fraud and emerging financial crime risks further into focus.

What does this mean for compliance teams?

It is time to move beyond checking whether a control exists and start asking:

1. Is the control operating as intended?
2. Is it identifying the risks it was designed to detect?
3. Are exceptions, alerts and red flags being investigated and escalated effectively?
4. Can we evidence the control's effectiveness?
5. Are identified weaknesses translated into meaningful remediation?

A policy can be well written. A screening system can be implemented. A transaction monitoring framework can be comprehensive on paper.

But if these fail to identify, prevent or escalate the risks they are designed for, their existence offers limited comfort.

The next phase of regulatory scrutiny is about effectiveness, evidence and accountability — not just implementation.

Perhaps the question every compliance function should be asking after October is:

If a regulator tested our controls tomorrow, would we be able to demonstrate that they actually work?

#AML #Sanctions #FinancialCrimeCompliance #RegulatoryCompliance #ComplianceEffectiveness

Impressive presentation..How US RTP works(US Real Time Payments)
A US company Fingrovia pays a contractor 5,000 USD on a Sunday night.
With US RTP®, the money lands in seconds. 

Here's what happens in that time 👇

1⃣ Fingrovia tells its bank (Citi) to pay John
2⃣ Citi sends a pacs.008 to the RTP network (run by The Clearing House)
3⃣ RTP checks it and passes it on to John's bank (Bank of America)
4⃣ BofA accepts and replies with a pacs.002 ✓
5⃣ The money settles straight away from a pre-funded joint account at the NY Fed
6⃣ Citi gets a pacs.002 confirming the payment is final, and John is credited
What stands out:
🔹 Open 24/7/365, including weekends and holidays
🔹 Up to $10 million per payment (raised from $1M in Feb 2025)
🔹 Push only: nobody can debit your account through RTP
🔹 Final and irrevocable. Mistakes can't be reversed automatically, only through a request for return (camt.056)
🔹 Built on ISO 20022, so the payment can carry rich, structured data

As users share credentials with personal AI agents, banks are struggling to distinguish between legitimate, authorised activity and agents acting beyond their instructions.

Shell and ExxonMobil have spent decades competing for lubricant customers.
But for 27 years, they have owned a lubricant additives company together.
Now they are reportedly considering selling it for $8 billion.

The company is Infineum.

Shell owns 50%. ExxonMobil owns the other 50%.

And Infineum is not some small chemical supplier.
Its additives go into engine oils and other lubricants used around the world. The company says its technology is present in roughly one-third of vehicles globally.

Think about that.

Two of the biggest competitors in lubricants have spent more than a quarter of a century jointly owning a business that supplies the industry.

Now both may walk away from that ownership.

The Financial Times reported that Bank of America has been engaged to explore a possible sale. Nothing has been concluded.

For those of us manufacturing lubricants, the interesting question is not simply who buys Infineum.

It is what the new owner might do.
Will it invest more aggressively in additive technology?
Will it pursue customers and markets differently?
Will the priorities change when the shareholders are no longer two of the world's largest oil companies?

A finished lubricant carries a brand on the drum.

But behind that drum are base oil suppliers, additive manufacturers, formulation approvals and years of technical development.

Most customers never see that part of the business.
Yet a change in ownership there could eventually matter across the entire lubricant industry.

Shell and ExxonMobil compete fiercely in the finished lubricant market.

For 27 years, they have also been business partners behind the scenes.

Sometimes the most interesting competition is between companies that are also partners.

Your AI agent gets hacked. Your bank says: "Not our problem."

This happened on Nov 18 and almost nobody is talking about it.

Citi, PNC and Citizens updated their customer terms. If you give a third-party AI agent access to your bank account, you are responsible for everything it does.

Even if the agent makes a mistake.
Even if the agent gets hacked.

JPMorgan and Bank of America made similar changes in October.

Citi made one exception: AI agents that Citi itself provides.

Think about what that means:
🤖 AI agents can now pay bills and move money
🔓 Every agent with your login is one more thing that can be attacked
💸 And the risk has moved from the bank to you

As someone who builds AI agents that call real APIs, here's the lesson for engineers:

Never design an agent that needs the user's password.

Use scoped, revocable access (OAuth-style tokens) instead.
Make the agent read-only by default.
Require human approval for every money movement.
Keep an audit log of every action.

Who pays when an agent fails is now the biggest open question in AI.

Would you give an AI agent access to your bank account after reading this? Yes or No? 👇

#AIAgents #AgenticAI #AI #CyberSecurity #FinTech #Banking #AIGovernance #TechNews

Your bank has just made you responsible for what your AI agent does. Read the clause before you connect one.

Citibank added a section to its online user agreement this month about third-party AI agents. It treats any action an agent takes as authorised by you, including where your credentials are, in its words, shared, leaked, or otherwise distributed to other AI agents. It also says the bank has no duty to investigate.

PNC changed its terms the same week. JPMorgan and Bank of America did it in October.

So the pattern is set. You connect the agent, that is your decision, and everything downstream is yours.

Now the part most coverage missed. There is no statute underneath this yet.

The banks are leaning on an old rule. Regulation E does not treat a transfer as unauthorised when a person you gave your access device to made it, and the official interpretation says that if that person exceeds your authority, you are fully liable.

Whether an AI agent, or the company running it, counts as that person is unsettled. Nobody has ruled on it.

Two things cut the other way. The same law stops banks contracting around your error-resolution rights. And the OCC's November bulletin classes autonomous payment agents as Tier 1 critical, which implies supervision rather than silence.

So the clause is the bank's opening position, not the final one.

Which is worth knowing, because a clause nobody reads becomes a precedent nobody argued.

If your agent got something wrong next month, would you know what you had agreed to?

Your customer's AI assistant just moved money. Who owns the mistake?

US banks have started to answer: the customer does.

This week Citi updated its online user agreement. Customers who give third-party AI tools access to their accounts are responsible for what those tools do, even if the tool is hacked. Citizens sent customers a similar warning, and PNC changed its terms on 18 November. JPMorgan and Bank of America announced similar policies in October.

Rewriting the terms is the easy part. The hard part lands on operations.

When a payment goes wrong, the dispute desk now faces questions it was never built for. Was it the customer or an agent? Was the agent authorised? Was the consent still valid?

Three things I would want every bank operations team to have ready:

-> A way to tell agent-initiated activity apart from customer-initiated activity.
-> A consent record showing what the customer allowed, and when it was revoked.
-> A dispute and fraud playbook written for agent errors, not just human ones.

Indian banking runs on UPI and account aggregators. As AI assistants start acting on customers' behalf, we will face this question too.

Better to design the answer in operations than discover it in a complaint.

Is your bank ready to tell a customer from their AI agent?

#BankingOperations #AgenticAI #DigitalPayments #RiskManagement #FutureOfBanking
